title: Leaders Raised by Wolves
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay explains why so many leaders unconsciously replicate the worst habits of their own mentors and role models, focusing on micromanagement as the most common example. It argues people mistake correlation for causation — assuming a mentor's heavy-handed oversight caused their success, rather than recognizing the mentor succeeded despite that flaw, through luck or overwhelming talent. The piece defines typical micromanaging tactics (presuming incompetence, demanding constant updates, requiring approval for everything) and their costs (demotivation, turnover, low morale), and urges leaders who recognize the pattern in themselves to deliberately break from what they learned rather than assume imitation equals success.
points: Argues micromanagement is most often learned by imitation from a prior mentor or role model, not chosen out of a need for control.
Identifies the core reasoning error: assuming a mentor's micromanaging style caused their success rather than being survived despite it.
Catalogs specific micromanaging tactics — presumed incompetence, constant status demands, requiring approval for everything — and their team-level costs.
Notes micromanagers often persist in the behavior for years even after clear negative feedback, because the belief in its necessity runs deep.
Closes by urging leaders to consciously reject harmful inherited behaviors rather than emulate every trait of an admired mentor.
quotes: It’s somewhat astounding how often leaders who play favorites, manage work-life balance poorly, have difficulty delegating to others, and express high emotions when they are frustrated have experienced those same tactics themselves from a leader or role model in their lives.
The odds are that if a leader had a previous manager or mentor who was a micromanager, they, too, resort to this coercive style.
Micromanagers in any industry or workplace share a common set of tactics. First and foremost, they presume team members are incapable of completing tasks without detailed guidance and supervision.
Of course, the real explanation is that the mentor succeeded despite their micromanaging, which means they had a lot of luck in the process or had such extreme talent that they overwhelmed this flaw.
Celebrating the role models we have admired and learned from by emulating their behaviors is what good leaders do. But only after they reject those tactics that are ineffective or harmful.
